entries.narration: Before we touch a single Databricks feature, it is worth asking what the finished data is for, because every decision in this course is judged against that. A data product is a table that somebody depends on, and the people who depend on it can feel four things: how fresh it is, how correct it is, what it costs, and who is allowed to read it. Take one feed of retail orders and three readers. The numbers on screen are assumptions I chose to show the trade-offs, not measurements from a real company. The finance team closes the books once a day. It needs yesterday's totals by six in the morning, right to the cent, with every order counted exactly once, and for finance a wrong number is far worse than a late one. The store dashboard is read all day long. Numbers about fifteen minutes old are fine, as long as the counts match what the tills saw, and here a late number is worse than a slightly rough one. The analyst studies years of history at once. Tomorrow is soon enough, but there must be no duplicates and no lost versions, because history that was thrown away cannot be rebuilt. Now look at the table at the bottom. Every one of those wishes has a price. Fresher data means more runs, or a stream that never stops, and that is paid in compute. Stricter correctness means checks, a quarantine and a reconciliation, and that is paid in latency. Longer history is paid in storage, and tighter access in engineering time. So one design rarely suits all three readers equally, and the first decision is whose need sets it. The common mistake is to assume fresher is always better. If finance reads a total once a day, refreshing it every fifteen minutes costs money and buys nothing. Keep the four questions on the right, because every course after this one comes back to them. Next, the three names you will meet everywhere: Spark, Delta and Databricks.

Three names come up in almost every Databricks conversation, and they are easy to blur together. The cure is to give each one exactly one job. Apache Spark is an engine. It takes a query, splits it into tasks, and runs those tasks across many machines at once, for SQL, for DataFrames and for streams. What Spark does not do is store anything. It reads files and writes files, and when the job ends, nothing of it remains except what it wrote. Spark has its own course in this series, so here we take only what we need. Delta Lake is a table format. It turns a folder of Parquet files into a table by writing a transaction log beside them. Because every change is a commit in that log, a write lands whole or not at all, and the table gains versions, history, MERGE and schema enforcement. It is important to see that Delta is files and a log. There is no Delta server running anywhere. Both Spark and Delta are open source, and this course runs both of them on an ordinary machine. Databricks is a platform, and a commercial service. It runs Spark and Delta for you, on compute it creates and manages, and it adds the things a team needs around them: Unity Catalog, which names every table and decides who may read it; ingestion tools, declarative pipelines and scheduled jobs; and the workspace, deployment and monitoring. Some of those, like Unity Catalog, also have open-source versions now, but in this course they are taught as the platform documents them. The table underneath is the test of whether the layers are clear. Running a query on fifty machines is Spark's job. Which files make up a table right now, or what it looked like yesterday, is answered by Delta's log. Who may read the gold table is Unity Catalog's question, and what starts the job at five in the morning is the job scheduler's. The last column says which course builds each answer. Next, the idea that ties these layers together: the lakehouse.

For a long time, a company that wanted both data engineering and business reporting ran two systems. On the left is that design. Raw files land in a data lake, which is cheap cloud storage that holds anything but offers no transactions, so two writers can leave a half-finished mess. Every night a copy job reshapes the files and loads them into a warehouse, a database with its own closed storage format, because that is where SQL and dashboards run well. It works, but notice what it costs. There are two copies of the data, kept in step by a job that can fail. Access rules are defined twice, once on the files and once in the warehouse. And the dashboards only see data after the nightly copy has finished. On the right is the lakehouse. There is one copy, in open files in your own cloud storage. Those files are Parquet with a Delta log beside them, so they get transactions directly, without a second database. One catalog sits over them and holds the names, the grants and the lineage. And every kind of engine reads that same copy: SQL and BI tools, Spark jobs and streams. The table at the bottom sums up what changes: one copy instead of two, open files throughout, transactions on the files themselves, access rules defined once, and SQL that sees a write as soon as it commits rather than the next morning. It is worth being honest about what a lakehouse does not remove, which is the list on the right. Raw files still have to be cleaned into good tables; that is most of this course. The size and arrangement of files still decide how fast queries run. And one copy only helps if nobody quietly makes a second one. The lakehouse is an architecture, not a product, and Databricks is one way of running it. Next, the most common way of organising the tables inside it: bronze, silver and gold.

Inside a lakehouse, tables are often organised in layers called bronze, silver and gold. Bronze keeps what arrived, as close to the source as possible. Silver makes it trustworthy. Gold answers one business question. Rather than describe them, let's push eight real orders through all three. These tables come from a local run of Spark and Delta, the same versions this whole course uses. Bronze, on the left, holds eight rows, and every column is text, because bronze does not judge. Look closely and you will find two problems. Order four appears twice, a resend with identical values. And order seven has the amount n slash a, which is not a number at all. To build silver, the job casts the store and the amount to real types, keeps one copy of each identical row, and refuses any row whose amount cannot be read as a decimal. Silver has six rows. Gold keeps only the completed orders and adds them up per store. Store seven has two orders and sixty-five. Store nine has one, for fifteen, because its other order was cancelled. Store twelve has one, eighty. The total is one hundred and sixty. Now the step that people skip: account for every row. Eight rows in bronze equals six in silver, plus one resend that was merged, plus one row that was rejected. If those numbers did not add up, we could not trust anything downstream. Here is the caution that matters most, and it is the table on the right. Calling a table silver guarantees nothing. That a write lands whole comes from the Delta log. That only finance can read gold comes from Unity Catalog grants. That order seven is set aside and counted, rather than silently lost, comes from the job's quality rules. And that gold is fresh by six comes from the schedule and its alerts. Each of those is a course of its own. And not every flow needs three layers; use the pattern where it helps. Next, the project we will build.

Databricks is a big platform, and a tour of its features would be long and forgettable. So instead we will build one project, a retail lakehouse, from an empty folder, and learn each part of the platform at the moment the project needs it. This is the finished project. On the left are its sources, landed in cloud storage. Order files arrive from the stores, one file per arrival, and sometimes the same order is sent twice. A change feed carries customer updates: new customers, changed addresses, and deletions. And a small reference table maps stores to cities: seven is Leeds, nine is York, twelve is Hull. In the middle are the Delta tables, all named and governed in one catalog. Bronze keeps what arrived. Silver is typed, deduplicated and enriched, with bad rows quarantined rather than lost. Customers keep their full history. And gold holds sales per city and per day. Under each piece is the course where we build it. On the right are the consumers from the first section, reading gold through grants. The table is gold for the sample day after the whole course's cleaning rules have run: Leeds seventy-five from three orders, York fifteen, Hull eighty. The middle band is how the project runs on the platform: as a declarative pipeline, as a scheduled job, measured for speed and cost, and deployed with a bundle and tests. I should be clear about one thing now, because it applies to the whole course. Everything that open-source Spark and Delta can do, we actually run, and every number on screen is what that run printed. What only the platform can do, like grants, Auto Loader, pipelines and jobs, is shown as real configuration from the project, checked against the documentation, and labelled as documented rather than run. Around the project are the courses about the platform itself, about table reliability, change, and finally defending the whole design. Next, how the platform actually runs your code.

When you log in to Databricks and run a query, three different places are involved, and they belong to two different accounts. Knowing which is which answers most questions about security and cost before they are asked. This frame follows the Databricks documentation for AWS; none of it is something we run in this course. On the left is the control plane. It lives in Databricks' own cloud account, and it is everything Databricks operates for you: the web application and the API, the workspace configuration, your job definitions and schedules, the cluster manager that starts compute, and Unity Catalog, which holds the names of your tables and who may read them. In the middle is the compute plane, where data is actually processed, and it comes in two kinds. Classic compute is virtual machines in your own cloud account, inside your own network. You pay the cloud provider for the machines, and Databricks for its units of work on top. Serverless compute runs in Databricks' account instead, in the same region as your workspace. Databricks starts and sizes it, there are no machines for you to manage, and there is one bill. On the right is your cloud storage: buckets in your own account. Every table's files live here, the Parquet data and the Delta log, along with the landing zone for raw files, and a workspace storage bucket for the platform's own system data, logs and results. Read the table at the bottom with our project in mind. The nightly job's definition and schedule are in the control plane. The machines that run it are in whichever compute plane you choose. Bronze, silver and gold are files in your bucket. And the rule that says who may read gold lives in Unity Catalog. So, as the list says, your data at rest stays in storage you own, the code runs wherever the compute is, and storage and compute are separate bills and separate decisions. Next, the boundaries above a single workspace.

A single query runs inside a workspace, but the workspace is not the top of the tree, and it is not the boundary most people assume it is. This frame is the documented structure, drawn for our retail company. The names on it are ours, not a real account. At the top is the account. It holds billing, it holds every workspace, and it holds identities. Users like Ana, groups like finance and store managers, and service principals, which are identities for software, like the one our scheduled job will run as. Identities are managed once, at the account, and then assigned to the workspaces they need. Inside the account is the metastore, and there is one per region. It is Unity Catalog's top-level container, and it holds every catalog of data in that region. Both of our workspaces sit in the same region, so they attach to the same metastore. Retail dev is where we build, and retail prod runs the scheduled job and serves the dashboards. Now the important part. Because both workspaces share one metastore, a table is not inside a workspace. The data lives in catalogs, and a catalog can be bound to particular workspaces. Here the development catalog is visible only in dev, and the production catalog is bound to prod, and readable but not writable from dev. The table on the right lists the boundaries and what each one separates. The account separates billing, users and regions. The metastore holds every catalog in a region. A workspace separates notebooks, jobs and compute. A catalog binding decides which workspace sees which data. And underneath it all, the cloud account separates buckets and networks. Three mistakes follow from this, and they are in the list. A workspace is not a data boundary. A grant follows its identity into every attached workspace. And development is separated from production with catalogs and bindings, not by copying data. Course 4 builds all of this. Next, the compute that actually runs our code.

Databricks offers several kinds of compute, and the most useful way to tell them apart is to ask two questions: what is it made for, and what does it cost while it is doing nothing? The table at the top answers both, from the documentation. I will not quote prices or start-up times, because they change with the cloud, the region and the plan. An all-purpose cluster is for notebooks and exploring, often shared by a few people. Its machines are in your account, and it keeps billing while idle until it auto-terminates. Job compute is created for one run of a job and removed when the run ends, so there is no idle time to pay for. A classic or pro SQL warehouse serves SQL and dashboards from machines in your account, and bills until it auto-stops. A serverless SQL warehouse does the same job on Databricks' machines, and its auto-stop can be set much shorter. And serverless compute for notebooks, jobs and pipelines keeps no machines waiting for you at all. Now apply it to our project, in the table at the bottom left. This is a provisional choice, and Course 11 revisits it with measurements. Ana, building the project, explores in notebooks on a small all-purpose cluster with a short auto-termination, so an evening away does not cost a night of machines. The nightly job that builds bronze, silver and gold runs on job compute or serverless jobs, which exist only while it runs. The store dashboards query all day, so they get a SQL warehouse. And finance's single query at six in the morning uses that same warehouse, which is already there. A few words you will meet are on the right. A DBU is the unit Databricks bills compute in. Auto-termination stops an idle cluster after a number of minutes. Access mode decides whether a cluster is shared, called standard, or dedicated to one user, and Unity Catalog needs one of the modes that support it. Next, what actually runs on that compute: the Databricks Runtime.

Every cluster and every job on Databricks runs a Databricks Runtime, and it is worth knowing what is inside one, because this course does not use it. A Runtime is a release, chosen per cluster or per job. According to its release notes, each one pins a version of Apache Spark, and bundles Delta Lake with some table features that only Databricks has, along with Auto Loader, the connection to Unity Catalog, the optional Photon engine, and a version of Python and Java with a set of libraries already installed. Long-term support releases are maintained for longer than the others, and serverless compute chooses the version for you. On the right is what this course runs instead, and these values are from a real run. Python three point one three. PySpark four point zero point one, and the engine underneath it, Spark four point zero point one. Delta Lake four point zero point zero. OpenJDK twenty-one. And the master is local with two threads: one machine, two parallel tasks. Everything here is open source, and from Course 3 on, every course builds exactly this session. Why run it locally at all? Because the table at the bottom splits the platform into two halves. Spark SQL, DataFrames and streaming behave the same in both, and so do the Delta log, MERGE, history and VACUUM. Those we run, and every number on screen is what the run printed. File counts and task counts depend on how many machines did the work, so they are never compared with a cluster's. Unity Catalog and grants, Auto Loader, pipelines and jobs, Photon and predictive optimization exist only on the platform. Those are shown as the real configuration they would take, checked against the documentation, and labelled as documented rather than run. If you have a workspace, you can follow along there, and the same code will run. Just check which Spark version your Runtime pins. Next, a single query's path through the platform, and why its name has three parts.

Let's follow one query, select everything from retail dot silver dot orders, and see who answers each question along the way. Across the top is the path on the platform, as the documentation describes it. The name has three parts: the catalog, retail, the schema, silver, and the table, orders. The compute does not know where that table is. It asks Unity Catalog, which resolves the name, and checks that this user holds three privileges: use catalog on retail, use schema on silver, and select on the table. If any one is missing, the query stops here with a permission error, before a single file is touched. If all three are present, Unity Catalog returns the table's location in cloud storage, together with a short-lived credential that is scoped to that table's files and nothing else. Only then does the compute read the files from your bucket. So the catalog is not just a list of names. It is the gate between every query and the data. Below it is the same thing tried locally, and these lines and errors are from a real run. A local session has exactly one catalog, called spark catalog. A two-part name, silver dot orders, works and finds its one row, in a folder under the local warehouse directory. The three-part name fails, with the error that spark catalog requires a single-part namespace but got retail dot silver. And a grant statement is not even valid syntax locally. There is no one to grant anything to. This is why the course writes names in two ways. Code that runs uses two parts, because that is what the local session resolves. Code that is documented uses Unity Catalog's three parts, because that is what you would write on the platform. The table beside it says where each answer comes from: which table a name means, whether a user may read it, and where its files are. On the platform, Unity Catalog answers all three. Locally, nobody checks the second one at all. Next, where your code is written, and where it runs.

The last question about the platform is a practical one: where do you write your code, and where does it run? They are not always the same place. The table at the top lists the documented options. A notebook in the workspace runs on whatever compute it is attached to, and keeps its own revision history. A Git folder in the workspace holds the same notebooks and files, but versions them with real Git, with branches, commits and pulls. With your own editor and Databricks Connect, the code is on your laptop, but each query is sent to remote compute in the workspace, through Spark Connect. With your editor and local Spark, which is what this course does, both the code and the compute are on your machine. And in Course 12, a bundle deploys the code as jobs and pipelines. Below it, on the left, is what a notebook really is, underneath. When a workspace exports a Python notebook as source, it is a plain Python file. The first line says it is a Databricks notebook. Each cell is separated by a line that reads command, followed by dashes. And a cell in another language, like markdown or SQL, is kept as comment lines that start with the word magic. This one explores the bronze orders, first in Python, then with a SQL query that counts them by status. Notice that it uses the platform's three-part names, and the display function that only a workspace provides, so this one is documented, not run. Course 3 runs a notebook in this format locally. The list beside it is the choice this course makes. Code lives in files, in Git, from the next course on. It runs locally, on open-source Spark and Delta. Notebooks are for exploring, and the job imports a real Python package rather than living inside a notebook. On a workspace, the same files would sit in a Git folder, unchanged. That completes the picture of the platform. Next, we start the project itself, from an empty folder.

From here on, every lesson happens inside one project, and it helps to see the whole of it once before we build it from nothing. This is retail lakehouse as it will look at the end of the course. Down the left is the project as your editor shows it. In the middle, where code will normally be, is a table of what each part is for and which course builds it. The virtual environment and the requirements file hold Spark and Delta for running locally, and the session module is the one place the project starts Spark. Both are this course. The governance folder holds the grants that say who may read what, in Course 4. The data folder is where files land, in Course 6. The heart of the project is the package under source, retail: one module per layer, bronze, silver and gold, built in Courses 6 and 7, a quality module with the rules and the reconciliation, and a module for changes and history in Course 8. The pipelines folder declares the same tables as a declarative pipeline in Course 9. The resources folder and databricks dot yml describe the job, the pipeline and the bundle that deploys them, in Courses 10 and 12. Tools hold the sample data and, later, a generator for a million orders. And the tests run on every change. Notice the shape: it is a Python package with a few folders around it, not a pile of notebooks. That is what lets the same code run on your laptop today and as a scheduled job on the platform later. On the right is how to read every lesson from now on. The project is on the left, with new files marked and the open file highlighted. The code is in the middle, with this lesson's lines lit up. Under it is the terminal, exactly as it really ran. A line with three dots folds away what the lesson does not need. And anything that only the platform can run is marked as documented, not run. Next, we make the folder and install Spark and Delta.

We start from an empty folder, and five commands turn it into a project, all in the terminal at the bottom. First we make the folder and move into it. Then python dash m venv creates a virtual environment, the project's own copy of Python, and activating it means every python and pip in this terminal now uses that copy instead of the machine's. Next we install two packages, each pinned to an exact version: pyspark four point zero point one, which is Spark itself, and delta-spark four point zero point zero, which is Delta Lake's Python side. Pinning matters. A project that says only pyspark gets whatever version is newest on the day it is installed, and then a frame in this course might not match what you see. Then pip freeze writes down everything that was installed into requirements dot txt, which is the file in the editor. Five lines. Our two pins are there, and so are three packages they brought with them: py4j, which lets Python talk to Spark's JVM, and importlib metadata with its own helper, zipp, which delta-spark needs. Anyone who installs from this file gets exactly these versions. The last command checks Java. Spark runs on the Java virtual machine, so Python alone is not enough, and Spark four needs Java seventeen or twenty-one. This machine has OpenJDK twenty-one. The list on the right says what we have and have not got yet. pyspark brings Spark with all of its own Java jars. delta-spark brings only Delta's Python functions. Delta's Java jars are not on the machine yet: they arrive the first time a session asks for them, which is the next lesson. On Databricks, none of these commands are needed, because the Runtime already contains Spark, Delta and Java. Locally, these five lines are the whole of the setup. Next, the session that speaks Delta.

Every program that uses Spark starts by building a Spark session, and this project builds it in exactly one place: the session module in the retail package. Every job, tool and notebook will call build session, so a change to how Spark starts is made once. The project has grown around it. The conf folder holds Spark's logging and defaults, so the terminal shows warnings only. pyproject dot toml makes the folder an installable Python package, and the first command in the terminal installs it in editable mode, so import retail works from anywhere in the project and edits take effect immediately. Look at the highlighted lines in the builder. Two config lines turn plain Spark into Spark that speaks Delta. The extension adds Delta's SQL commands, like MERGE, VACUUM and DESCRIBE HISTORY. Replacing the default catalog with Delta's catalog means that a table we create is a Delta table. Enable Hive support gives the session a catalog that is saved on disk, so a table we name today still has that name in tomorrow's run. It is a local stand-in for what Unity Catalog does on the platform. And the last line passes the builder through configure spark with delta pip, which tells Spark to fetch Delta's Java jars. That is what most of the lines in the terminal before our output are. The very first is a notice from Java about an incubating module, which every Spark four run on Java twenty-one prints; the Spark course explains it. The rest come from Delta's jars. Spark uses a tool called Ivy to find those jars on Maven Central and keep them in a folder in your home directory. The first run downloads them. Every later run finds them there, and the report's last line says so: nothing copied, three already retrieved. Spark prints this report on every start, so from the next lesson on, the notice and the report are folded into one line. Then our own output: Spark four point zero point one, Delta four point zero point zero, the local master with two threads, Delta's catalog in place, and a warehouse folder inside the project, where tables will be written. On Databricks, the Runtime already has Delta's jars and a governed catalog, so none of this configuration is needed. Next, the first table.

Now we write a table. The tool in the editor holds the eight sample orders from the first course, exactly as they arrived: every column is text, order four was sent twice, and order seven has an amount of n slash a. Bronze keeps all of that, because bronze does not judge. The highlighted lines build a DataFrame from those rows, create a schema called bronze, and save the data as a Delta table named bronze dot orders. The terminal confirms eight rows. Now look at what that one write left on disk. Spark wrote the table into the warehouse folder, under bronze dot db, then orders. Inside are two Parquet files holding the rows. There are two because our session runs two tasks at once, and each task wrote its own file. A different machine could write a different number, which is why this course never quotes file counts. Beside the data is the folder that makes this a Delta table: the delta log. It holds version zero of the table as a JSON file, a checksum of that version, and a folder that Delta four creates and leaves empty here. The last command lists the kind of each action in version zero, one per line. A commit record says what operation made it. Metadata holds the schema. Protocol says which Delta features a reader needs. And then one add action for each data file. That is the whole idea of Delta in five lines: the table is not the folder. It is the list of files that the log says belong to it. A reader asks the log, not the folder listing, which is why a half-written file that never reached the log is never read. The name bronze dot orders lives somewhere else entirely, in the local metastore folder that has appeared at the top of the project. Course 5 reads every version of this log. Next, the first query against it.

With a table in place, we can ask it a question: how many orders are in each status? The tool in the editor asks it twice, once in each of the two languages this course uses. The first is SQL. Select the status and a count, from bronze dot orders, grouped by status and ordered by it. The second is PySpark, the DataFrame API: take the table, group by status, count, and order. The table on the right lines the two up clause by clause, and they say exactly the same thing. Neither one has run yet when it is written. Each builds a plan, and only an action, like show or collect, makes Spark execute it. That is why the tool can build both and then compare them. The terminal shows the answer. One cancelled, six completed and one pending, eight in all. And the last line is the comparison: PySpark gives the same rows. They do, because both spellings become the same plan inside Spark, so choose whichever reads better for the job in hand. This course mixes them freely, and Course 7 shows where each one is the clearer choice. Now look at that answer once more, because it is the reason the next ten courses exist. Six completed orders. But one of those six is order four's resend, and another is order seven, whose amount is not a number. A finance report built straight on this table would count orders that should not be counted, and would fail to add up an amount that is not there. The query is correct. The data underneath it is not yet fit to answer the question. Bronze is what arrived, and a question like this one belongs on silver, after the rules have been applied. Next, the same exploration as a notebook.

On a workspace, exploration like this usually happens in a notebook, and the last lesson of this course shows what a notebook really is. The file in the editor is in the notebook source format from Course 2. The first line tells a workspace to open it as a notebook. Each line that reads command, followed by dashes, starts a new cell. And the lines that begin with magic hold a cell in another language, here a markdown heading. Everything else is ordinary Python. That means we can run it locally as a plain script, and the terminal shows it doing exactly that. There is one difference, and the second cell's comment points it out. On a workspace, a variable called spark already exists in every notebook. Locally nothing creates it, so this notebook builds the session itself, the same way every job does. The table on the right lists the markers and what each one means on a workspace. The third cell asks three questions of bronze. How many rows? Eight. How many different order IDs? Seven, because order four was sent twice. And how many completed orders have an amount we can actually add up? Only four: orders one, two, four and five. Order seven is completed, but its amount is n slash a. Order three was cancelled, and order six is still pending. So eight rows in bronze become four good sales, and the gap between those two numbers is the work ahead: deciding, in code, which rows count, and accounting for every one that does not. That is silver, in Course 7. The project now has a session, a table, a query and a notebook, all running locally. Before we bring in any more data, we need to decide who is allowed to read it. Next, governance with Unity Catalog.

Before any more data arrives, we decide what it will be called and who may touch it, because both are much harder to change later. On Databricks, both are the job of Unity Catalog, and this course is entirely documented rather than run, since Unity Catalog needs a workspace. The tree across the top is how it names things, from left to right. At the top is the metastore, one per region, which we met in Course 2. Inside it are catalogs, the first part of every name. Our company has two with the same shape: retail for production, and retail dev for building. Inside a catalog are schemas, the second part. Retail has bronze, silver and gold, one per layer. And inside a schema are the objects themselves, the third part: tables like orders and sales, volumes that hold files, like landing, and views, which are saved queries. So a table's full name has three parts, catalog, schema and table, like retail dot silver dot orders. The code below it shows the two ways to write one. The fully qualified name always means exactly one table, wherever it runs. Or a session can set a default catalog and schema, and then use the last part alone. Defaults are convenient in a notebook, and dangerous in a job, because the same short name means a different table depending on what was set before it. That is also how development and production stay apart: the same code, pointed at retail dev or at retail. The table beside the code connects this to what we actually run. Our local session has a single catalog, so the tables we created in Course 3 have two-part names: bronze dot orders, silver dot orders, gold dot sales. When you see a three-part name in this course, it is configuration for the platform, documented. When you see two parts, it is code that really ran, against a local catalog kept in a Derby database. Next, the three kinds of object a schema can hold.

A schema in Unity Catalog can hold three kinds of object, and each is reached, and granted, in its own way. The table at the top lists them, from the documentation. A table holds rows with a schema, and you reach it by its three-part name. Reading it needs the select privilege. A view holds no data at all. It is a saved query over other tables, reached by name like a table, and it needs select on the view itself. And a volume holds files, any files in any format, and you reach it by a path that starts with slash Volumes, followed by the catalog, the schema and the volume's name. Reading it needs a different privilege, read volume. The last column says where each one lives in this course's project, because we run locally: the tables are the ones in our local catalog, a view is a temporary view in a session, and the role of a volume is played by the data landing folder, which arrives in Course 6. The two cards underneath show the same landing data reached two ways. On the left, through a table, with SQL against its name: the rows have already been parsed, typed and governed. On the right, through a volume, by reading the raw CSV files at their path: nothing has been parsed yet, and the reader decides how. Both are documented here. The table at the bottom lists the privilege each object needs: select to read a table or a view, modify to write a table, read volume and write volume for files, and on a schema, use schema, plus the right to create tables and volumes in it. The list beside it is how to choose. Data that arrives as files should land as files, in a volume, so there is always an untouched copy of what came in. Everything from bronze onwards is a table. A view is the way to share a question, a filtered or aggregated slice, without making a copy that can drift. And because each object is granted separately, a person can be allowed to read the gold table without being able to open the raw files behind it. Next, the difference between a table whose files the catalog owns and one whose files you own.

Every table has files somewhere, and the question this lesson answers is: who owns them? The answer decides what happens when the table is dropped. There are two kinds of table. A managed table has no location in its definition. The catalog chooses where its files go, and the catalog looks after them. An external table names its own location, and those files belong to whoever owns that path. This difference is not just platform documentation, because our local catalog behaves the same way, and the tool in the editor proves it. It makes two copies of bronze orders. The first, highlighted, is managed: no location, so its folder appears inside the warehouse. The second is external: it is created at a path we chose, under data slash external. The tool checks that both folders exist, drops both tables, and checks again. The terminal shows the result of a real run. Before the drop, both folders are there. After it, the managed table's folder is gone, files and all. The external table's folder is still there, and reading it directly still finds all eight rows. Dropping an external table removes only the name. The table on the right puts that next to the platform's documented behaviour. On Unity Catalog, managed tables live in storage the catalog controls, and when one is dropped its files are removed after a period, during which the undrop command can bring it back. External tables live in an external location, which comes up two lessons from now, and dropping one never touches the files. So which should you use? Managed, for the tables you build: bronze, silver and gold. The catalog can then optimize them and clean up after them. External, for data that another system writes or owns, where deleting the files would be someone else's decision. Locally, a drop deletes at once, so treat a managed table's drop as final. Course 12 returns to deleting data on purpose. Next, who is allowed to do any of this.

Now the project gets its first platform-only file: governance slash grants dot sql, open in the editor. It is documented, not run, because grants need Unity Catalog. A grant gives a privilege on an object to a principal, and there are three principals here, listed on the right. Finance and data engineers are groups of people, and the retail job is a service principal, an identity for software, which the scheduled job will run as. Grant to groups rather than to people, so that when someone joins or leaves, you change a group, not twenty grants. Read the file top to bottom. Finance gets use catalog on retail, then use schema and select on the gold schema, and nothing else. Data engineers get all privileges on bronze and silver, where they build. And the retail job can read bronze, and read and modify silver, which is exactly what its job needs. That is least privilege: each principal gets what its work requires, and no more. The rules that turn these lines into permissions are documented, and the list on the right states them. Reading a table needs three things at once: use catalog on its catalog, use schema on its schema, and select. A grant on a schema covers every table inside it. Since we cannot run Unity Catalog, the terminal runs a small model of those rules, in tools slash grant matrix, which reads this very file and works out who can do what. It is a model, not Unity Catalog, but it makes the consequences visible. Finance can read gold and nothing else. Engineers can read and write bronze and silver, but not read gold. And the retail job can read bronze and silver, and write silver, but cannot see gold. The last lines show a refusal and why: finance reading silver orders lacks use schema on silver, and select. On the platform that is a permission error, raised before a single file is read. Course 10 comes back to this when the job needs to publish to gold. Next, how a governed table reaches files in cloud storage.

Grants decide who may use a table. But a table is files in a cloud bucket, and the cloud has its own permissions. This lesson follows how Unity Catalog bridges the two, as the documentation for AWS describes it. The names on screen, like the partner's bucket, are made up. Across the top is the chain. It starts with an IAM role in your own cloud account, which is allowed to read a particular bucket. Unity Catalog never hands that role to users. Instead, an administrator registers it as a storage credential: Unity Catalog's handle on the role. A storage credential is created from the role in the catalog's interface or through the API, which is why it is not drawn as SQL. Then an external location pairs one credential with one path. And on that location you can create external tables or volumes, and grant them like any other object. The code underneath is the documented SQL for the last steps. Create an external location called partner feed, at the partner's path, using the partner role credential. Grant read files on that location to the data engineers, so they can list and read what lands there. And create an external table, bronze partner orders, on a folder under it. Notice what never appears: no access key, no secret, no cloud permission in anyone's hands. The table on the right lists the three separate controls that every access passes through, and any one of them can say no. The workspace decides who can log in and run anything at all. Unity Catalog decides who may use which object. And cloud IAM decides what the role itself can reach. A user with a grant but no workspace access gets nothing. A role that cannot reach the bucket fails every grant on top of it. And the list explains why the chain is worth the trouble. Users never hold cloud keys. There is one role per location, not one per person. And revoking a grant in the catalog closes the path at once. Next, the evidence that governed data leaves behind.

Governance is not only saying no. It is also being able to answer questions afterwards: what is this table, where did it come from, and who has touched it? Unity Catalog records the evidence for all three, and this lesson shows where it lives, from the documentation. Across the top is lineage for our gold table. Files land in the landing volume, bronze orders is loaded from them, silver orders is built from bronze, and gold sales is built from silver. Nobody draws this by hand. Unity Catalog captures it as queries run on the platform, from the tables each query read and the table it wrote. The query underneath asks the lineage system table what fed retail gold sales, newest first. System tables are tables the platform maintains about itself, and an administrator has to enable them before they can be queried. The column names here should be checked against the current documentation before you rely on them. The table on the right sorts the evidence into three kinds. Metadata answers what something is and who owns it: names, owners, comments and tags, which is what people search when they are trying to discover the right table. Lineage answers what fed what, and it is kept in the lineage system table. Audit answers who did what and when: every grant, every query, every change, kept in the audit system table. Underneath is an illustrative result, not a real run: one row saying silver orders fed gold sales. The value of lineage shows up on a bad day. If a number in gold is wrong, lineage tells you which tables to inspect, and in what order. If a source is about to change its format, lineage tells you everything downstream that will break. And when someone asks who could have seen a column of personal data last month, audit answers it with records rather than memory. Locally, our Delta tables keep their own history, which Course 5 reads. Next, how to use data that belongs to someone else.

The last governance question is about data you do not own. Suppose a partner sells our products and has its own orders. There are three documented ways to bring them in front of a query, and they differ in whether the data is copied, how fresh it is, and who pays. The first is to ingest it: copy it into our bronze layer, the way Courses 6 and 7 do with our own files. We then own a copy, governed like any of our tables. It is only as fresh as the last load, and we pay to store and to load it. The second is Delta Sharing. The partner grants us access to their table, and our compute reads their files directly, with no copy on our side. It is as fresh as the partner's last commit, the partner stores it, and the partner can revoke access at any time. The third is Lakehouse Federation. The partner's data stays in their own database, and each query we run is sent to that database to answer. It is as fresh as the source, every single time, but every query also puts load on their system, which is fine for a quick look and risky for a job that runs every night. The table at the bottom puts the trade side by side. Only ingesting copies the data. Sharing and federation are live, but in different ways: one reads the provider's files, the other runs the query on the provider's system. In all three cases the result is governed in our catalog, so the grants from this course apply. The list on the right is what to ask before choosing. How fresh must it be? Who pays to read it? May the data leave its source at all, for legal or contractual reasons? And how much load can the source take? For this course the answer is ingest, because the retail lakehouse needs its own history and its own checks. Governance is now in place. Next, we make the tables themselves reliable, starting with what a Delta table really is.
